prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks reaching 10^-18 precision
for the detection of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the opening of neutrino astronomy with the IceCube detector

statement.case_for: I have moved from my opening first place, WMAP, to a two-part prize that pairs optical lattice clocks (B015) with IceCube (B040). Both pass the test I care about most: nature supplied a clue and an instrument was built to read it. The lattice clocks are the broadest-supported entry on the table (six members ranked it, two first-place), their attribution is the cleanest in the shortlist (Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's record accuracy), and independent laboratories agree with one another at the 10^-18 level. That cross-checking, between clocks rather than between theories, is the maturity I look for, and it opens new observables: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, constancy of constants, dark-matter searches. IceCube opened a new window on the universe, a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux since 2013 and source evidence in TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane. The two parts are distinct (laboratory precision measurement and observational astrophysics) and total three people, which fits the statutes.
statement.case_against: The weakest point is B040 as a solo credit. IceCube is a very large collaboration, AMANDA and earlier pioneers are not in the credited names, and the individual source identifications are still at moderate significance, so naming one person risks looking arbitrary. For B015 the reservation is that it is an increment in precision on prizes already given for combs (2005) and ion clocks (2012), and that a metrology prize is a tool-and-measurement prize rather than a discovery. A combined prize also looks like a compromise between two unrelated fields. If the committee cannot defend single-name credit for IceCube, B028 or B013 would be the more discovery-centred partners, although they need three names each and cannot be combined with B015 under the three-person limit.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clocks first because they improve the best instrument for time by two orders of magnitude over caesium and open new ways of observing nature, with Katori and Ye as a clean pair confirmed by many labs.
responses.response: I agree with this and it is what moved me towards B015, since it satisfies the criterion that discoveries come first: new observables follow from the clock, not just a better number. Where I would press you is the redefinition of the second, which has not happened. I would not lean on it. The case should rest on the fundamental-physics reach already demonstrated, and the citation should name the invention and realisation of the lattice clock, not a future SI outcome.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B015 first, as precision atomic physics that redefines what can be measured, but flags that the Hall/Hänsch and Wineland lineage leaves the committee needing to say what is new.
responses.response: That is the right question and I think it has a good answer. The 2005 and 2012 prizes gave us the comb and single-ion control. The lattice clock is a different principle, the magic wavelength, which lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once with Doppler and recoil removed, giving a new regime of statistical power rather than a faster version of the same idea. I would still want your expert view on whether the ion-clock community would accept that framing, because a commissioned external report should test it, not me.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a new observational window, with sources now identified, but is candid that a sole-laureate configuration is unfair given the collaboration and the AMANDA and Baikal pioneers.
responses.response: I share your doubt about single-name credit and I do not wave it away. My view is that Halzen's role as the conceiver of the cubic-kilometre ice detector and long-time leader is unusually identifiable for a collaboration-scale project, which is why I put him forward. But I would accept that if experts show the credit needs more people, B040 cannot share a prize with B015 and the configuration would have to change. I also note that you ranked WMAP last of your list for being overshadowed by COBE, Planck and the 2019 prize, which is a fair point against my own opening choice, and part of why I now treat B028 only as an alternative.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a new door opened by tuning one parameter, with Bistritzer and MacDonald predicting and Jarillo-Herrero observing.
responses.response: I ranked B017 sixth in my own opening, so I am not dismissive: the prediction followed by a clear experimental clue from nature is exactly what I admire. My reservation, which you share, is the unsettled pairing mechanism and the unresolved credit among experimental groups (Cao, Dean, Young, Efetov, Yacoby). A prize for the platform before the interpretation settles is slightly early, and I would rather it ripen than risk a citation that later looks wrong. I would not oppose it in a later year, and I would like the condensed-matter members to say what a citation would actually claim.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as an architecture behind superconducting quantum processors and a clean demonstration of basic quantum phenomena, while flagging overlap with the 2025 prize and the Blais exclusion.
responses.response: I appreciate your candour about proximity to that community. My concern is the one you raise yourself: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close in subject, and a four-name credited set that forces the exclusion of Blais, the lead theory author, makes the attribution uncomfortable. I take the fundamental-physics content seriously, but the committee should not give a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon unless the cavity-QED regime is shown to be a distinct discovery. I would hold B012 for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether single-name credit for Halzen can be defended given the size of IceCube and the AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES predecessors.
Whether lattice clocks are judged a new principle or an increment on the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Whether pairing laboratory metrology with neutrino astronomy is acceptable as two distinct achievements sharing one prize.
Whether the committee prefers a discovery-centred cosmology or gamma-ray burst prize (B028 or B013) over either part, once expert reports are in; I rely on memory for the credit details of both.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are not credited on any shortlisted entry, and I have no known tie to the credited individuals. I note that my own research on de Sitter space and dark energy gives me an interest in cosmology (B028), which I disclose as an intellectual bias, not an institutional conflict.
